content: Drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) is a significant global health challenge, particularly when the causative strain of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is resistant to rifampicin, the most effective first-line anti-TB drug. This resistance may also extend to isoniazid, another key first-line drug, and in some cases, to at least one fluoroquinolone, such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) refers to TB caused by strains resistant to rifampicin, which may also exhibit resistance to other firstor second-line TB medications. Isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) is characterized by resistance to isoniazid while remaining susceptible to rifampicin. Serious adverse events in TB treatment are defined as those that result in death, life-threatening conditions, hospitalization, prolonged hospitalization, significant disability, or congenital anomalies. Events requiring intervention to prevent these outcomes are also included. Such events may necessitate discontinuation of the suspected drug. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes conditions such as miliary TB, TB meningitis, osteoarticular TB, or pericardial TB. In children under 15 years, extrapulmonary forms other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal masses without compression) are considered severe. TB disease in humans is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which includes eight closely related organisms, such as M. tuberculosis, M. bovis, and M. africanum. Among these, M. tuberculosis is the most common and clinically significant cause of human TB. A TB case refers to the occurrence of TB disease in an individual, while a TB patient is someone receiving care for TB. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed consolidated guidelines for the treatment of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), which are updated based on the latest evidence. These guidelines aim to address the challenges posed by DR-TB, which is more difficult to treat than drug-susceptible TB and threatens global progress toward TB elimination targets. The guidelines emphasize evidence-based recommendations for the treatment and care of DR-TB patients, including the use of shorter, all-oral regimens and novel drugs like bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid. The WHO's 2022 update includes recommendations for the use of a 6-month regimen (BPaLM: bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin) for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) patients, as well as a 9-month all-oral regimen for those without fluoroquinolone resistance. Longer regimens (18–20 months) are suggested for patients with more extensive resistance profiles. The guidelines also address the timing of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-positive TB patients, the role of surgery in TB management, and the monitoring of treatment response through sputum culture and smear microscopy. The WHO emphasizes the importance of using effective treatment regimens tailored to the patient's resistance profile and clinical condition. For example, all three Group A agents (bedaquiline, linezolid, and a fluoroquinolone) should be included in longer regimens, along with at least one Group B agent. Injectable agents like kanamycin and capreomycin are no longer recommended due to their toxicity. The guidelines also highlight the need for monthly sputum culture monitoring and the inclusion of ART for all HIV-positive TB patients. The development of these guidelines involved rigorous evidence review using the GRADE approach, which assesses the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The recommendations aim to improve treatment outcomes, reduce adverse events, and support national TB programs in implementing effective DR-TB management strategies. The WHO continues to prioritize research and innovation to address gaps in knowledge and improve the global response to DR-TB.
